newsitem.title: USA: Democrats sought $7 million from Asian-Americans.
newsitem.headline: Democrats sought $7 million from Asian-Americans.

text.p: The Democratic Party on Monday released documents describing a master plan to raise $7 million in 1996 campaign funds from Asian-Americans.

The objective, one paper said, was to unite the party and President Bill Clinton's White House in wooing an Asian-American community that was "growing rapidly and could be a reservoir for votes and contributions in 1996."

While there is nothing illegal about soliciting campaign funds from any particular group of American citizens, the disclosure seemed sure to fuel suspicions that some Democratic fund-raisers may have used Asian-Americans as cover in funnelling illegal funds from foreign sources to party coffers.
It also further undermined Clinton's original effort to distance the White House from party fund-raising schemes.

The party has already returned $1.5 million in illegal or improper funds in a controversy that has plagued Clinton almost since his re-election last November, with another $1.5 million or so to come. Much of that came from Asian interests.

The latest disclosure came to light among some 10,000 pages of internal documents released by the Democratic leadership group, the Democratic National Committee, in what appeared to be an effort in advance damage control.
The documents, provided in three large cartons to news organisations that paid an $846 copying fee, were copies of papers subpoenaed by a congressional investigating committee.

The one outlining the Asian-American fund-raising effort, dated April 1996, said in part: "The National Plan has set an overall fundraising goal for the APA (Asian Pacific American) community as $7 million for the 1996 election cycle."
"This election cycle will be a time when APAs will come of age -- politically."
It said one of members of an APA working group anchoring this drive was John Huang, then a key Democratic fund-raiser who has become a central figure in the controversy.
Huang is said to have raised several million dollars for the re-election of Clinton and Vice President Al Gore.
He is a former executive of the Lippo Group financial conglomerate of Indonesia, some of whose top officials are friends of Clinton from his days as governor of Arkansas.

The documents showed that the party organised an Asian Pacific American Working Group, including Huang, in January and February of 1996 "to draft a strategic plan (hereinafter the 'national plan') to coordinate all White House, Democratic National Committee and Clinton-Gore 1996 activities for the Asian Pacific American community."
The document "targeted" as "key states" California, New York, Illinois, Washington, Texas, Hawaii, New Jersey, Virginia and Massachusets.

It noted that there were "legal constraints" involving White House fund-raising that did not apply to the party, but said the White House office of Asian Pacific Affairs "shall complement" efforts by Democratic fund raisers.
Among the controversies in the unfolding fundraising row is the solicitation of guests invited to the White House for coffees with Clinton and for overnight stays.

Gore has admitted making telephone calls to contributors from the White House but he said he used a campaign credit card and denied violating laws forbidding government officials to solicit funds from government offices.

One of the documents released on Monday was an 11-page briefing paper for Gore for a breakfast for 80 to 100 donors of at least $12,500 from the Asian American community at a Washington hotel on Feb. 20, 1996.

The breakfast for the Asian American Leadership Council was organised by Huang and the briefing paper said Gore's role was to discuss the presidential campaign and "inspire political and fundraising efforts among the APA community."
The latest DNC documents showed the party kept meticulous track of big contributors, proposed government jobs for fund raisers and promoted White House tours for donors.
